title: Star on a Hubble diet
caption: The star cluster Pismis 24 in the nebula NGC 6357, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Pismis 24, Pismis 24-1 · constellation Scorpius · about 8000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA and Jesús Maíz Apellániz (Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía, Spain). Acknowledgement: Davide De Martin (ESA/Hubble)

recognition.text: Official ESA/Hubble press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: The bright stars in this Hubble image belong to Pismis 24, a small open cluster sitting at the heart of NGC 6357, a large emission nebula, in the direction of Scorpius. The nebula spans one degree on the sky. Intense ultraviolet light from the cluster's hottest stars heats the surrounding gas and has blown a bubble in the nebula.

Pismis 24-1, a bright young star in the cluster's core about 8,000 light-years from Earth, had been one of the leading candidates for the Milky Way's heaviest star. It was thought to weigh an astonishing 200 to 300 times as much as the Sun.

New Hubble measurements changed that picture. They resolved Pismis 24-1 into two separate stars, which roughly halved its mass estimate to around 100 solar masses. The cluster's youngest, bluest heavyweights ionise part of the nebula, and the surrounding gas clouds make the region harder to study.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.62 x 4.22 arcminutes) and distance (8000 light years), the frame spans roughly 6.1 × 9.8 light-years. Its light set out about 8,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, using visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view split what looked like one star into two, a separation far beyond what the eye could make.

explore: An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that glows because nearby hot stars energise it. This image combines data from two Hubble cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and the Wide Field Planetary Camera 2, including filters that isolate glowing hydrogen.
alt: A group of bright stars in the core of a glowing nebula.
